Cyrus the Great. Around 600 to 530 BCE, Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Empire, creating the ancient world's first truly multinational state spanning from Egypt to India. Known for his military genius and administrative tolerance, he unified the Persian kingdoms and extended his rule through conquest and negotiation, leaving a legacy that shaped the political imagination of empires for millennia.

Born into the Anshanid dynasty, Cyrus seized power from the Median overlords and unified the Persian tribes. His military conquests acquired the wealth of the known world. He conquered the Lydian kingdom under Croesus around 546 BCE, acquiring Asia Minor's riches. Then in 539 BCE, he captured Babylon without destruction, positioning himself as a liberator rather than a conqueror, and the Cyrus Cylinder records his remarkably tolerant policies.

What set Cyrus apart was his administrative vision. He established the Achaemenid Empire as a vast system divided into satrapies, each governed by a satrap answerable to the king. He allowed conquered peoples to practice their own religions and maintain local laws, an unprecedented policy of cultural pluralism. He recruited local elites and capable administrators into his government, integrating Babylonian, Egyptian, and Median traditions into a cosmopolitan court. He created a royal road system connecting the empire from Sardis to Susa, facilitating communication and military movement across vast distances.

His tolerance and administrative genius created an empire that survived him for two centuries, making him one of history's most successful empire-builders by the longevity of his creation. Greek historians revered him as a model ruler; Xenophon idealized him in the Cyropaedia. Cyrus died while campaigning on the northeastern frontier, having founded an empire that would dominate the Near East for generations to come.
